results.title: Incident identification
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines methods and channels for identifying and tracking serious incidents across the model lifecycle, including consideration of external sources and facilitation of third-party reporting.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework acknowledge and describe approaches for identifying serious incidents, including monitoring external sources and enabling third-party reporting?
expected_evidence: The framework explicitly recognises the need to identify and track serious incidents across the model lifecycle.
The framework describes intended methods for identifying serious incidents, including reference to post-market monitoring or similar processes.
The framework references consideration of external information sources (e.g. media, incident databases, research, public reporting).
The framework describes how downstream providers, users, or other third parties may report serious incidents to the Signatory and/or authorities.
results.reasoning: None of the four expected indicators are clearly present in the text. The framework mentions lifecycle risk management and third-party monitoring but does not explicitly identify or track serious incidents, post-market monitoring, external information sources, or reporting channels for third parties to Signatories/authorities; thus operational indicators are unmet and cannot be offset by thematic alignment.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle risk management (GOV, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)
Monitoring of third-party resources (MANAGE 3.1)
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit acknowledgment of the need to identify and track serious incidents across the AI model lifecycle (GOV, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE).
Defined methods for identifying serious incidents, including post-market monitoring or equivalent processes.
Explicit consideration of external information sources (e.g., media, incident databases, research, public reporting).

Procedures and channels for downstream providers, users, or other third parties to report serious incidents to Signatories and/or authorities, including how reports are submitted, processed, and used.
Operational details such as timelines, retention periods, and responsibilities related to incident reporting and tracking.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The AI RMF acknowledges lifecycle risk management and monitoring of third-party resources, but does not explicitly describe methods for identifying/tracking serious incidents or channels for third-party reporting to Signatories or authorities.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: Partial conceptual alignment: lifecycle risk management and third-party monitoring are present, but explicit identification/tracking of serious incidents and reporting channels are not described.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle risk management (GOV, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)
Monitoring of third-party resources (MANAGE 3.1)

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The AI RMF mentions lifecycle risk management and third-party monitoring but does not explicitly define methods to identify or track serious incidents, nor channels for third-party reporting or use of external sources as required by the EU requirement.
missing_elements: Explicit acknowledgment of the need to identify and track serious incidents across the AI model lifecycle (GOV, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE).

results.title: Incident documentation
results.requirement: Describe whether and how the framework defines the information that should be tracked, documented, and reported for serious incidents, including root cause analysis, mitigation failures or circumvention, and handling of incomplete information.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework specify the minimum information set for serious incident documentation and reporting, including root cause analysis and treatment of missing information?
expected_evidence: The framework defines the categories of information to be documented for serious incidents (e.g. timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, and response actions).
The framework specifies that a root cause analysis should be conducted, including examination of model outputs, inputs, and any failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations.
The framework describes how patterns or signals from post-market monitoring may inform incident analysis.
The framework acknowledges that some information may be unavailable at the time of reporting and requires such gaps to be explicitly recorded.
The framework indicates that the level of detail in serious incident documentation should be proportionate to the severity of the incident.
results.reasoning: Evidence shows post-deployment monitoring and incident tracking/communication (MANAGE 4.x) but there is no explicit minimum information set, root-cause analysis, handling of incomplete information, or severity-based documentation granularity. These missing indicators cannot be offset by thematic alignment alone.
key_aligned_concepts: Post-deployment AI system monitoring plans
Incidents and errors communicated to relevant AI actors
Processes for tracking, responding to, and recovering from incidents and errors
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit categories of information to document for serious incidents (e.g., timing, harm, affected groups, model involvement, response actions)
Root cause analysis requirements, including examination of model outputs, inputs, and failures or circumvention of systemic risk mitigations
Mechanism to use patterns or signals from post-market monitoring to inform incident analysis
Explicit recording and handling of information gaps when data is unavailable at the time of reporting
Proportionality guidance: level of detail in incident documentation commensurate with incident severity

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The AI RMF includes post-deployment monitoring and incident tracking/communication processes (MANAGE 4.1 and 4.3) but does not specify a minimum information set for serious incidents, nor explicit root-cause analysis, handling of missing information, or proportionality of documentation as required by the EU requirement.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: Partial operational alignment: it covers incident tracking, reporting, and post-deployment monitoring, but it does not define the explicit information categories or root-cause/missing-information handling called for in the EU requirement.

evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Shows that the framework supports post-deployment monitoring, incident tracking, and communication, which are prerequisites for serious-incident documentation.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Operational incident tracking and reporting mechanisms (not the explicit information categories or root-cause/missing information handling)

gap_analysis.gap_summary: EU requires an explicit minimum information set for serious incidents, including root cause analysis, handling of incomplete information, and proportionality to severity. The AI RMF provides general post-deployment monitoring and incident tracking but lacks explicit information categories, root-cause analysis, handling of missing data, and severity-based detail guidance.

results.title: Reporting timelines
results.requirement: The framework defines mandatory severity-based reporting timelines for serious incidents involving the model, including differentiated deadlines for initial reports based on incident type, requirements for periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and submission of a final report after incident resolution.
results.assessment_question: Does the framework specify clearly differentiated reporting timelines for serious incidents (including specific deadlines for initial notification based on severity), periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents, and a final report after resolution?
expected_evidence: The framework defines categories of serious incidents (e.g., critical infrastructure disruption, cybersecurity breach, death, serious harm to health, fundamental rights, property or environment).
The framework associates specific deadlines for initial reporting following awareness of a serious incident (e.g., two days, five days, ten days, fifteen days depending on severity).
The framework clarifies that reporting is triggered when the organisation becomes aware of the involvement of its model, including cases of reasonable suspicion of causal linkage.
The framework specifies periodic intermediate updates for unresolved serious incidents (e.g., at least every four weeks after the initial report).
The framework defines a deadline for submitting a final report after resolution of the serious incident (e.g., within 60 days after resolution).
The framework allows aggregation of multiple similar serious incidents within defined reporting timelines while respecting the earliest applicable deadline.
results.reasoning: None of the six Expected Evidence indicators are present in the retrieved text: defined categories of serious incidents, severity-based initial reporting deadlines, awareness-based reporting triggers, periodic updates for unresolved incidents, final-resolution reporting deadline, and aggregation rules. The framework provides only high-level risk management guidance with no prescriptive incident-reporting obligations. Therefore, the requirement is not satisfied and thematic alignment cannot compensate for missing operational obligations.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Defined categories of serious incidents (e.g., critical infrastructure disruption, cybersecurity breach, death, serious harm to health, fundamental rights, property or environment).
Specific initial reporting deadlines differentiated by incident severity/type (e.g., two days, five days, ten days, fifteen days).
Reporting trigger based on organizational awareness of involvement of the model (including reasonable suspicion of causal linkage).
Requirements for periodic intermediate updates for unresolved incidents (e.g., at least every four weeks).
Deadline for submitting a final report after resolution (e.g., within 60 days after resolution).
Ability to aggregate multiple similar incidents within defined timelines while respecting the earliest applicable deadline.

Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

results.assessment_question: Does the framework define retention requirements for serious-incident documentation that meet or exceed a five-year period?
expected_evidence: The framework states that documentation of information related to serious incidents must be retained.
The framework specifies a minimum retention period of at least five years.
The framework indicates that the retention period is counted from the later of the documentation date or the date of the serious incident.
results.reasoning: None of the three Expected Evidence indicators are present in the retrieved text (retention of serious-incident documentation, a minimum five-year retention period, and retention calculation from the later of doc date or incident date). Missing a minimum retention period of at least five years for serious-incident documentation.
Missing retention period calculation anchored to the later of the documentation date or the incident date.
Missing an explicit governance/operational obligation to define, maintain, and implement these retention requirements.

The framework should also define how key systemic risk decisions and justifications are documented.

Documentation defines requirements for describing model integration into AI systems (where applicable).
Documentation defines requirements for documenting model evaluations, results, and evaluation strategies.
Documentation defines requirements for documenting implemented safety mitigations.
Documentation defines how key systemic risk processes, decisions, and justifications are recorded.
Documentation specifies retention periods for additional documentation (e.g. at least 10 years).
results.reasoning: None of the six Expected Evidence indicators are evidenced in the framework text: explicit binding requirements for maintaining architecture documentation, integration documentation, evaluation documentation/strategies, safety mitigations, systemic risk processes/justifications, and a defined 10-year retention with AI Office access are absent. The existing versioning/living-document governance reflects conceptual alignment but does not satisfy the operational, retention, or AI Office-access obligations required.

results.title: Public transparency
results.requirement: Define when and how summarised public versions of the Framework and Model Reports are published for the purpose of systemic risk assessment and mitigation, including safeguards to protect sensitive information and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations. The framework should also define conditions under which public publication is not required (e.g. similarly safe or safer models).
results.assessment_question: Does the framework define conditions, scope, safeguards, and exceptions for publishing public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports?
expected_evidence: The framework states that summarised versions of the Framework and Model Reports may be published.
The framework indicates that publication is required when necessary for systemic risk assessment or mitigation.
The framework indicates that removals or redactions are applied to protect sensitive commercial information and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations.
The framework states that Model Report summaries include high-level descriptions of systemic risk assessment results and safety and security mitigations.
The framework defines exceptions where publication is not required for similarly safe or safer models.
results.reasoning: All five Expected Evidence indicators are absent in the retrieved text. The gap analysis identifies missing elements: publishing conditions and process for public summaries, safeguards for sensitive information and mitigation efficacy, redaction/removal procedures, explicit publication exceptions (e.g., for similarly safe models), and linkage of summaries to systemic risk assessment. Without these operational mechanisms, thematic alignment cannot compensate.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No definition of when public summaries should be published (timelines, triggers, responsible parties).
No defined safeguards to protect sensitive information or ensure effectiveness of safety and security mitigations in summaries.
No procedures for redactions/removals of sensitive or commercially confidential information in summaries.
No explicit exceptions where publication is not required (e.g., similarly safe or safer models).
No specification that summaries serve systemic risk assessment/mitigation, including high-level content of systemic risk in Model Report summaries.
No alignment to external requirements, audience scope, or regulatory interaction specifics.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: No, the retrieved text does not define conditions, safeguards, scopes, or exceptions for publishing public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: There is no explicit alignment to the EU requirement. The text discusses governance, audience engagement, and versioning but does not define when/how public summaries should be published or permit redactions/exceptions.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The retrieved text lacks any explicit policy on publishing public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports, including when/how to publish, safeguards, redactions, or exceptions. It also does not tie publication to systemic risk assessment/mitigation or define exemptions for similarly safe/safer models.
missing_elements: Definition of when public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports should be published and the process for doing so (timelines, triggers, and responsible parties).
Defined safeguards to protect sensitive information and to ensure the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations in public summaries.
Procedures for redactions/removals of sensitive or commercially confidential information in summaries.
Explicit exceptions where publication is not required or is optional (e.g., when models are similarly safe or safer).
Specification that summaries serve systemic risk assessment and mitigation purposes, including what high-level content constitutes 'systemic risk' descriptions in Model Report summaries.
Clarity on alignment to external requirements, including the intended audience and interaction with regulatory expectations.
weaker_areas: Publication governance exists in general terms (audience, versioning) but there is no binding publication obligation or safeguards specifically for public summaries.
No binding criteria for publication thresholds or redaction standards; governance text does not translate into external publication controls.
scope_divergences: Divergence from EU requirement by not defining publishing conditions, safeguards, or exceptions for public summaries, nor linking publication to systemic risk assessment/mitigation.

synthesis_result.justification: All five Expected Evidence indicators are absent in the retrieved text. The gap analysis identifies missing elements: publishing conditions and process for public summaries, safeguards for sensitive information and mitigation efficacy, redaction/removal procedures, explicit publication exceptions (e.g., for similarly safe models), and linkage of summaries to systemic risk assessment. Without these operational mechanisms, thematic alignment cannot compensate.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No definition of when public summaries should be published (timelines, triggers, responsible parties).
No defined safeguards to protect sensitive information or ensure effectiveness of safety and security mitigations in summaries.
No procedures for redactions/removals of sensitive or commercially confidential information in summaries.
No explicit exceptions where publication is not required (e.g., similarly safe or safer models).
No specification that summaries serve systemic risk assessment/mitigation, including high-level content of systemic risk in Model Report summaries.
No alignment to external requirements, audience scope, or regulatory interaction specifics.

Map
The MAP function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system. The AI
lifecycle consists of many interdependent activities involving a diverse set of actors (See
Figure 3). In practice, AI actors in charge of one part of the process often do not have full
visibility or control over other parts and their associated contexts. The interdependencies
between these activities, and among the relevant AI actors, can make it difficult to reliably
anticipate impacts of AI systems. For example, early decisions in identifying purposes and
objectives of an AI system can alter its behavior and capabilities, and the dynamics of deployment setting (such as end users or impacted individuals) can shape the impacts of AI
system decisions. As a result, the best intentions within one dimension of the AI lifecycle
can be undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later activities.

This complexity and varying levels of visibility can introduce uncertainty into risk management practices. Anticipating, assessing, and otherwise addressing potential sources of
negative risk can mitigate this uncertainty and enhance the integrity of the decision process.

Map
The MAP function establishes the context to frame risks related to an AI system. The AI
lifecycle consists of many interdependent activities involving a diverse set of actors (See
Figure 3). In practice, AI actors in charge of one part of the process often do not have full
visibility or control over other parts and their associated contexts. The interdependencies
between these activities, and among the relevant AI actors, can make it difficult to reliably
anticipate impacts of AI systems. For example, early decisions in identifying purposes and
objectives of an AI system can alter its behavior and capabilities, and the dynamics of deployment setting (such as end users or impacted individuals) can shape the impacts of AI
system decisions. As a result, the best intentions within one dimension of the AI lifecycle
can be undermined via interactions with decisions and conditions in other, later activities.
Page 24
NIST AI 100-1
AI RMF 1.0
This complexity and varying levels of visibility can introduce uncertainty into risk management practices. Anticipating, assessing, and otherwise addressing potential sources of
negative risk can mitigate this uncertainty and enhance the integrity of the decision process.

system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.

criteria.title: Framework updates
criteria.requirement: Describe how the Safety and Security Framework defines the conditions, processes, and scope for periodic and event-driven framework assessments and updates, including versioning, changelogs, and remediation planning, in line with Measure 1.3 of the Safety and Security Chapter.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define how and when framework assessments and updates are intended to occur, including assessment triggers, periodic review, evaluation of framework adequacy and adherence, and the handling of remediation and versioning?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that it is subject to periodic reassessment (e.g. at defined intervals) and to reassessment when specified conditions or events occur.

The framework describes conditions or triggers that would lead to a framework assessment (e.g. material changes in model development, serious incidents or near misses, materially changed systemic risks or model capabilities).
The framework explains the scope of a framework assessment, including the evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to the systemic risks of the models.
The framework explains that framework adherence is assessed, including consideration of non-adherence and its causes.
The framework describes how findings from a framework assessment may lead to updates of the framework to keep it state-of-the-art.
The framework describes that updates are intended to be versioned and accompanied by a changelog explaining the nature and rationale of changes.
The framework describes how remediation plans are intended to be defined when framework assessments identify risks of continued or future non-adherence.
criteria.reasoning: Indicators 1, 5, and 6 are evidenced (periodic/regular cadence hints and versioned updates with changelogs, plus living-document framing). Missing indicators 2, 3, 4, and 7; no explicit assessment triggers, defined scope of framework assessments, evaluation of adherence, or remediation planning are described, and while updates are described, there is no formal mechanism tying assessment findings to updates or remediation.
key_aligned_concepts: Versioned updates with changelogs
Living document / periodic update cadence
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit assessment triggers for framework assessments
Defined periodic reassessment intervals for the framework itself
Defined scope of a framework assessment including adequacy with respect to systemic risks
Process for assessing framework adherence and identifying non-adherence causes
Defined mechanism showing how assessment findings lead to updates (rationale and prioritization)
Remediation planning for non-adherence (objectives, owners, timelines, follow-up)

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: The text describes versioning, changelogs, and a living-document update approach but does not clearly specify assessment triggers, periodic review intervals, evaluation of framework adequacy/adherence, or remediation planning.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: Partial alignment. It covers versioned updates and a living-document cadence, but lacks explicit assessment triggers, adequacy/adherence evaluation, and remediation planning details.
key_aligned_concepts: Versioned updates with changelogs
Living document / periodic update cadence

evidence_citations.quote: Framework will employ a two-number versioning system to track and identify major and minor changes. The first number will represent the generation of the AI RMF and its companion documents (e.g., 1.0) and will change only with major revisions. Minor revisions will be tracked using .n after the generation number (e.g., 1.1). All changes will be tracked using a Version Control Table which identifies the history, including version number, date of change, and description of change.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Direct evidence of structured versioning and changelog-like history tracking.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Updates are intended to be versioned and accompanied by a changelog (versioning and history tracking).

evidence_citations.quote: NIST plans to update the AI RMF Playbook frequently. Comments on the AI RMF Playbook may be sent via email to AIframework@nist.gov at any time and will be reviewed and integrated on a semi-annual basis.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Demonstrates a scheduled cadence for updates and integration of feedback.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Periodic updates and semi-annual integration; implies regular review cycles.

evidence_citations.quote: Be a living document. The AI RMF should be readily updated as technology, understanding, and approaches to AI trustworthiness and uses of AI change and as stakeholders learn from implementing AI risk management generally and this framework in particular.
evidence_citations.why_it_matters: Supports the concept that updates are expected and ongoing, aligning with the idea of periodic and event-driven refinement.
evidence_citations.indicator_addressed: Be a living document; readiness for updates as change occurs.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The external framework lacks explicit assessment triggers, defined periodic reassessment of the framework itself, and remediation planning; it emphasizes versioned updates and a living-document approach but does not clearly articulate how assessment findings drive updates or remediation.
missing_elements: Explicit assessment triggers for framework assessments (e.g., material changes in model development, serious incidents/near misses, materially changed systemic risks or model capabilities).
Defined periodic reassessment intervals for the framework itself and a formal process for performing them.
Explicit scope of a framework assessment, including evaluation of framework adequacy with respect to the systemic risks of the models.
Process for assessing framework adherence, including identification of non-adherence and its causes.
A defined mechanism showing how findings from a framework assessment lead to updates of the framework (including rationale and prioritization).
Remediation planning for identified risks of continued or future non-adherence (remediation objectives, owners, timelines, and follow-up).
weaker_areas: The text mentions versioning, changelogs, and a living-document cadence, but the periodic assessment cadence for the framework itself is not clearly defined (the described cadence mainly pertains to Playbook updates).
There is no explicit linkage or documented process tying assessment outcomes to concrete framework updates or remediation actions.
scope_divergences: No explicit description of assessment triggers for framework assessments (e.g., material changes, incidents, or systemic risk shifts).
No explicit definition of the scope and evaluation criteria for framework adequacy and adherence within framework assessments.
Remediation planning is not described within the framework assessment and update process.

criteria.requirement: Define and maintain additional detailed documentation describing the model’s architecture, integration into AI systems, evaluation approaches and results, and implemented safety mitigations, and ensure such documentation can be provided to the AI Office upon request and is retained for at least ten years after market placement. Documentation defines requirements for describing model integration into AI systems (where applicable).
Documentation defines requirements for documenting model evaluations, results, and evaluation strategies.
Documentation defines requirements for documenting implemented safety mitigations.
Documentation defines how key systemic risk processes, decisions, and justifications are recorded.

criteria.title: Public transparency
criteria.requirement: Define when and how summarised public versions of the Framework and Model Reports are published for the purpose of systemic risk assessment and mitigation, including safeguards to protect sensitive information and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations. The framework should also define conditions under which public publication is not required (e.g. similarly safe or safer models).
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define conditions, scope, safeguards, and exceptions for publishing public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports?
expected_evidence: The framework states that summarised versions of the Framework and Model Reports may be published.
The framework indicates that publication is required when necessary for systemic risk assessment or mitigation.
The framework indicates that removals or redactions are applied to protect sensitive commercial information and the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations.
The framework states that Model Report summaries include high-level descriptions of systemic risk assessment results and safety and security mitigations.
The framework defines exceptions where publication is not required for similarly safe or safer models.
criteria.reasoning: All five Expected Evidence indicators are absent in the retrieved text. The gap analysis identifies missing elements: publishing conditions and process for public summaries, safeguards for sensitive information and mitigation efficacy, redaction/removal procedures, explicit publication exceptions (e.g., for similarly safe models), and linkage of summaries to systemic risk assessment. Without these operational mechanisms, thematic alignment cannot compensate.
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No definition of when public summaries should be published (timelines, triggers, responsible parties).
No defined safeguards to protect sensitive information or ensure effectiveness of safety and security mitigations in summaries.
No procedures for redactions/removals of sensitive or commercially confidential information in summaries.
No explicit exceptions where publication is not required (e.g., similarly safe or safer models).
No specification that summaries serve systemic risk assessment/mitigation, including high-level content of systemic risk in Model Report summaries.
No alignment to external requirements, audience scope, or regulatory interaction specifics.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: No, the retrieved text does not define conditions, safeguards, scopes, or exceptions for publishing public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: There is no explicit alignment to the EU requirement. The text discusses governance, audience engagement, and versioning but does not define when/how public summaries should be published or permit redactions/exceptions.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The retrieved text lacks any explicit policy on publishing public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports, including when/how to publish, safeguards, redactions, or exceptions. It also does not tie publication to systemic risk assessment/mitigation or define exemptions for similarly safe/safer models.
missing_elements: Definition of when public summaries of the Framework and Model Reports should be published and the process for doing so (timelines, triggers, and responsible parties).
Defined safeguards to protect sensitive information and to ensure the effectiveness of safety and security mitigations in public summaries.
Procedures for redactions/removals of sensitive or commercially confidential information in summaries.
Explicit exceptions where publication is not required or is optional (e.g., when models are similarly safe or safer).
Specification that summaries serve systemic risk assessment and mitigation purposes, including what high-level content constitutes 'systemic risk' descriptions in Model Report summaries.
Clarity on alignment to external requirements, including the intended audience and interaction with regulatory expectations.
weaker_areas: Publication governance exists in general terms (audience, versioning) but there is no binding publication obligation or safeguards specifically for public summaries.
No binding criteria for publication thresholds or redaction standards; governance text does not translate into external publication controls.
scope_divergences: Divergence from EU requirement by not defining publishing conditions, safeguards, or exceptions for public summaries, nor linking publication to systemic risk assessment/mitigation.

synthesis_result.justification: All five Expected Evidence indicators are absent in the retrieved text. The gap analysis identifies missing elements: publishing conditions and process for public summaries, safeguards for sensitive information and mitigation efficacy, redaction/removal procedures, explicit publication exceptions (e.g., for similarly safe models), and linkage of summaries to systemic risk assessment. Without these operational mechanisms, thematic alignment cannot compensate.

No defined safeguards to protect sensitive information or ensure effectiveness of safety and security mitigations in summaries.

No explicit exceptions where publication is not required (e.g., similarly safe or safer models).

criteria.title: Risk identification process
criteria.requirement: Define a structured systemic risk identification process that is explicitly informed by the types of risks, the nature of systemic risks, and the sources of systemic risks as set out in Appendix 1, and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define a structured systemic risk identification process that is informed by the risk types (Appendix 1.1), the nature of systemic risks (Appendix 1.2), the sources of systemic risks (Appendix 1.3), and that explicitly considers the specified systemic risks (Appendix 1.4)?
expected_evidence: The framework describes a structured process for identifying systemic risks stemming from the model.

The framework indicates that potential systemic risks are initially considered with reference to the types of risks defined in Appendix 1.1 (e.g. risks to public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, and society).

The framework explains that the identification process considers the nature of systemic risks, including essential and contributing characteristics such as scale, propagation, capability-dependence, or irreversibility (Appendix 1.2).

The framework describes how potential sources of systemic risks are considered in the identification process, including model capabilities, model propensities, and model affordances or contextual factors (Appendix 1.3).

The framework explicitly indicates that the specified systemic risks listed in Appendix 1.4 are taken into account as part of the systemic risk identification process, such as risks related to chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) threats, loss of control of the model, large-scale cyber offence, and harmful manipulation.
criteria.reasoning: No indicators from the Expected Evidence are demonstrated in the text. The framework offers a generic risk-management lifecycle (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) but does not define a structured systemic risk identification process aligned to Appendix 1 risk types, nature, sources, or the specified Appendix 1.4 risks, leaving all indicators unmet.
key_aligned_concepts: Risk management lifecycle (MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: No defined, structured systemic risk identification process explicitly informed by Appendix 1.1 risk types.
No explicit consideration of Appendix 1.2 risk nature (scale, propagation, capability-dependence, irreversibility).
No explicit consideration of Appendix 1.3 risk sources (model capabilities, model propensities, model affordances, contextual factors).
No explicit incorporation of Appendix 1.4 specified systemic risks (e.g., CBRN threats, loss of model control, large-scale cyber offences, harmful manipulation).
No operational procedures mapping Appendix 1 risks to risk identification steps (responsibilities, timing, documentation).

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: No—the AI RMF does not define a structured systemic risk identification process explicitly informed by Appendix 1 risk types, nature, sources, or the specified systemic risks; it provides a high-level risk management framework (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) and references external standards rather than a tailored process based on Appendix 1 risks.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The framework offers a structured risk management lifecycle (MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) but does not explicitly operationalize Appendix 1-based systemic risk identification or enumerate the specified risks; alignment is thus limited to high-level governance and risk management concepts, not the detailed Appendix 1 requirements.
key_aligned_concepts: Risk management lifecycle (MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE)

It provides only a high-level risk-management lifecycle (GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE) without Appendix-1-tailored identification mechanisms.
missing_elements: A defined, structured systemic risk identification process explicitly informed by Appendix 1.1 risk types (e.g., risks to public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, and society).
Explicit consideration of the nature of systemic risks as per Appendix 1.2 (scale, propagation, capability-dependence, irreversibility).
Explicit consideration of the sources of systemic risks as per Appendix 1.3 (model capabilities, model propensities, model affordances, contextual factors).
Direct incorporation of the specified systemic risks listed in Appendix 1.4 (e.g., CBRN threats, loss of control of the model, large-scale cyber offence, harmful manipulation).
Operational procedures mapping Appendix 1 risks to risk identification steps (responsibilities, timing, documentation).
weaker_areas: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE provide general risk management rather than Appendix-1-based systemic risk identification.
Lack of binding, prescriptive requirements or metrics tied to Appendix 1 risk categories; no risk-type mapping or risk-source assessment procedures.
Reliance on external standards (e.g., NIST frameworks) rather than a tailored Appendix 1-aligned identification process.
scope_divergences: No explicit reference to Appendix 1.1–1.4 content; risk types, nature, sources, and specified systemic risks are not enumerated or operationalized.
The focus remains on governance and lifecycle processes rather than a dedicated systemic risk identification process.

organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

criteria.title: Model-independent information
criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines the gathering of model-independent information relevant to systemic risk analysis, including how the breadth and depth of information gathering are determined in relation to the systemic risk.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the organisation systematically gather and document model-independent information relevant to identified systemic risks, using structured methods such as web searches or OSINT, literature reviews, market analyses of comparable models, training data reviews, historical incident analysis, forecasting of technological trends, expert consultations, and/or stakeholder or community engagement?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that systemic risk analysis is informed by model-independent information.
The framework explains that the breadth and depth of model-independent information gathering are adjusted based on the characteristics or severity of the systemic risk.

The framework indicates categories of methods that may be used to gather model-independent information, such as web searches or open-source intelligence, literature reviews, market analyses, reviews of historical incident data, forecasting of general trends, expert interviews or panels, and participatory or community-based research methods.

The framework clarifies the role of model-independent information in informing subsequent stages of systemic risk analysis (e.g. evaluations, modelling, or estimation), without requiring that such stages have already been performed.
criteria.reasoning: Evidence exists that external engagement and model-independent information inform risk management (indicators 1 and 4) and that breadth/depth adjustments based on risk characteristics are referenced (indicator 2). However, there is no explicit, EU-aligned catalog of information-gathering methods (e.g., OSINT, literature reviews, market analyses, training data reviews, etc.), and no clearly defined mechanism mapping model-independent information to subsequent systemic risk analysis stages, which leaves indicator 3 unmet. As these operational gaps cannot be compensated by thematic alignment alone, the overall status is PARTIALLY_COMPLIANT.

Part 1: Foundational Information
1.
Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,
such as threats to civil liberties and rights, while also providing opportunities to maximize
positive impacts. Addressing, documenting, and managing AI risks and potential negative
impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.
1.1
Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability
of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.
The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can be positive, negative, or both and can
result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the
negative impact of a potential event, risk is a function of 1) the negative impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs and 2) the likelihood of
occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,
and the planet.
“Risk management refers to coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk” (Source: ISO 31000:2018).

Part 1: Foundational Information
1.
Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,
such as threats to civil liberties and rights, while also providing opportunities to maximize
positive impacts. Addressing, documenting, and managing AI risks and potential negative
impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.
1.1
Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability
of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.
The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can be positive, negative, or both and can
result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the
negative impact of a potential event, risk is a function of 1) the negative impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs and 2) the likelihood of
occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,
and the planet.
“Risk management refers to coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk” (Source: ISO 31000:2018).

criteria.title: Risk estimation
criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines the estimation of the probability and severity of harm for systemic risks, using at least state-of-the-art risk estimation methods and taking into account relevant information inputs.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how the probability and severity of harm for systemic risks are intended to be estimated using state-of-the-art methods, taking into account relevant information from systemic risk identification, analysis, and serious incident reporting, and how such estimates are expressed?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that probability and severity of harm are estimated as part of systemic risk analysis.
The framework indicates that at least state-of-the-art risk estimation methods are used, appropriate to the systemic risk being assessed.

The framework explains that risk estimation takes into account relevant information inputs, such as outputs from systemic risk identification and analysis and information about serious incidents or near misses.

The framework describes how estimates of systemic risk are expressed, for example as risk scores, risk matrices, probability distributions, or other qualitative, semi-quantitative, or quantitative formats.
The framework explains the purpose of risk estimation in supporting systemic risk acceptance determination, without requiring specific numerical or qualitative results.
criteria.reasoning: Found indicator: probability and severity are described as part of systemic risk analysis (indicator 1). Missing indicators: (2) state-of-the-art estimation methods, (3) inputs from systemic risk identification/incident reporting, (4) explicit formats for expressing estimates, and (5) purpose linking estimation to systemic risk acceptance decisions. These operational elements are not present and cannot be compensated by general conceptual alignment.

Use of general risk management framing and alignment with standards (NIST/ISO)

criteria.title: Post-market monitoring
criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines post-market monitoring to gather information relevant to systemic risk assessment and updating, and how independent external evaluators are intended to be enabled under appropriate safeguards, where applicable.
criteria.assessment_question: What post-market monitoring methods are required for assessing and mitigating systemic risk, and under what conditions and safeguards must independent external evaluators be granted access to model versions, chains-of-thought, and safety-reduced model variants, including protections against legal retaliation and responsible vulnerability disclosure timelines?
expected_evidence: The framework describes that post-market monitoring is conducted to gather information about the model’s capabilities, propensities, affordances, and/or effects.
The framework explains that post-market monitoring informs systemic risk acceptability determinations and decisions on framework or report updates.

The framework indicates that a range of post-market monitoring methods may be used, such as collecting end-user feedback, providing reporting or incident channels, engaging with affected stakeholders, monitoring public sources, or supporting independent research.
The framework describes how post-market monitoring applies when the model is integrated into AI systems provided or deployed by the Signatory.
The framework describes whether and under what conditions independent external evaluators are intended to be provided with access to the model for post-market monitoring purposes.

The framework explains the safeguards associated with external evaluator access, such as selection criteria, information security measures, responsible disclosure procedures, and non-retaliation commitments.
criteria.reasoning: Found indicators: 1) post-market monitoring collects information on capabilities/behavior; 6) safeguards for external evaluators. Missing indicators: 2) explicit link between monitoring outcomes and framework/report updates (only risk management is shown), 3) explicit enumeration of monitoring methods, 4) explicit Signatory deployment applicability scope, 5) explicit access conditions to model versions/chains-of-thought/safety-reduced variants and associated timelines, 6) vulnerability disclosure timelines and data retention/framework-update triggers. Since the missing indicators are operational and not offset by thematic alignment, the overall assessment is only partially compliant.

Access safeguards for independent external evaluators (selection criteria, information security, responsible disclosure, non-retaliation)

No explicit conditions for external evaluators' access to models (including access to model versions, chains-of-thought, and safety-reduced variants) and timelines.
No defined vulnerability disclosure timelines and escalation procedures; no explicit data retention terms or framework/update triggers beyond generic remediation.

expected_evidence: The framework describes how systemic risk acceptance is determined for each identified systemic risk.
The framework defines systemic risk acceptance tiers or, where tiers are not suitable and the risk is not a specified systemic risk, alternative acceptance criteria.

Emerging knowledge and methods to better inform harm/cost-benefit tradeoffs will continue to be developed and debated by businesses, governments, academia, and civil society.
To the extent that challenges for specifying AI risk tolerances remain unresolved, there may

The Framework is intended to be flexible and to augment existing risk practices
which should align with applicable laws, regulations, and norms. Organizations
should follow existing regulations and guidelines for risk criteria, tolerance, and
response established by organizational, domain, discipline, sector, or professional
requirements. Some sectors or industries may have established definitions of harm or
established documentation, reporting, and disclosure requirements. Within sectors,
risk management may depend on existing guidelines for specific applications and

use case settings. Where established guidelines do not exist, organizations should
define reasonable risk tolerance. Once tolerance is defined, this AI RMF can be used
to manage risks and to document risk management processes.
1.2.3
Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

from risks that emerge in operational, real-world settings.
Inscrutability: Inscrutable AI systems can complicate risk measurement. Inscrutability
can be a result of the opaque nature of AI systems (limited explainability or interpretability), lack of transparency or documentation in AI system development or deployment, or
inherent uncertainties in AI systems.
Human baseline: Risk management of AI systems that are intended to augment or replace
human activity, for example decision making, requires some form of baseline metrics for
comparison. This is difficult to systematize since AI systems carry out different tasks – and

criteria.title: Proceeding decisions
criteria.requirement: Describe how the framework defines decisions to proceed with, restrict, or not proceed with the development, making available on the market, or use of the model based on systemic risk acceptance determination.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework describe how decisions to proceed or not proceed with the development, market availability, or use of the model are made based on systemic risk acceptance determination, and how responses are defined when risks are not acceptable or are likely to become unacceptable?
expected_evidence: The framework states that proceeding with development, making available on the market, or use of the model is conditional on systemic risks being determined acceptable.
The framework states that if systemic risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to soon become unacceptable, appropriate measures must be taken before proceeding.
The framework describes possible actions when risks are not acceptable, such as not making the model available on the market, restricting availability, withdrawing, or recalling the model.
The framework states that safety and/or security mitigations are to be implemented when systemic risks are not acceptable.

The framework states that another round of systemic risk identification, systemic risk analysis, and systemic risk acceptance determination is to be conducted when risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to soon become unacceptable.
criteria.reasoning: None of the five Expected Evidence indicators are present in the retrieved text; the framework discusses risk governance and tolerance at a high level but provides no explicit decision gates for proceeding/restricting/not proceeding based on systemic risk acceptance, nor defined responses to unacceptable risks or re-assessment cycles. Thematic alignment cannot compensate for missing operational indicators.

Core governance structure (GOV, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE) for addressing AI system risks
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Missing explicit decision gate: proceeding with development, market availability, or use based on systemic risk acceptance.
Missing defined responses when systemic risks are not acceptable (e.g., not making model available, restricting availability, withdrawing/recalling).
Missing mandatory safety/security mitigations tied to non-acceptable risks, with concrete implementation requirements and timelines.
Missing mandated re-assessment cycles: another round of systemic risk identification/analysis/acceptance with cadence and responsible authorities.
Missing documentation and accountability: explicit roles, responsibilities, decision authorities, audit trails.

gap_analysis.gap_summary: The external framework lacks explicit, binding decision gates to proceed/restrict/not proceed based on systemic risk acceptance, plus defined remedial actions when risks are not acceptable, and clear accountability for these decisions. It also does not specify timelines, triggers, or cycles for re-assessing systemic risk acceptance in light of changing risks.
missing_elements: Explicit decision gate: proceeding with development, market availability, or use of the model based on systemic risk acceptance (a formal, documented threshold and sign-off for proceed/not proceed).

Defined responses when systemic risks are not acceptable: actions such as not making the model available, restricting availability, withdrawing, or recalling the model, with clear triggers and authorities responsible for each action.
Mandatory safety and/or security mitigations tied to non-acceptable systemic risks, with concrete implementation requirements and timelines.

mandates for repeated cycles: another round of systemic risk identification, analysis, and acceptance determination when risks are not acceptable or are reasonably foreseeable to become unacceptable, including who conducts it and the cadence.

weaker_areas: Risk tolerances and alignment with laws/regulations are discussed as governance inputs but are not binding decision thresholds or procedural criteria for proceeding with deployment.

Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because

prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the

NIST AI 100-1
AI RMF 1.0
Part 1: Foundational Information
1.
Framing Risk
AI risk management offers a path to minimize potential negative impacts of AI systems,
such as threats to civil liberties and rights, while also providing opportunities to maximize
positive impacts. Addressing, documenting, and managing AI risks and potential negative
impacts effectively can lead to more trustworthy AI systems.
1.1
Understanding and Addressing Risks, Impacts, and Harms
In the context of the AI RMF, risk refers to the composite measure of an event’s probability
of occurring and the magnitude or degree of the consequences of the corresponding event.
The impacts, or consequences, of AI systems can be positive, negative, or both and can
result in opportunities or threats (Adapted from: ISO 31000:2018). When considering the
negative impact of a potential event, risk is a function of 1) the negative impact, or magnitude of harm, that would arise if the circumstance or event occurs and 2) the likelihood of
occurrence (Adapted from: OMB Circular A-130:2016). Negative impact or harm can be
experienced by individuals, groups, communities, organizations, society, the environment,
and the planet.
“Risk management refers to coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to risk” (Source: ISO 31000:2018).

Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

criteria.title: Safety mitigations
criteria.requirement: The framework defines and requires the implementation of safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle that are appropriate to identified systemic risks, sufficiently robust under adversarial pressure, and taking into account the model’s release and distribution strategy, with the objective of ensuring that systemic risks are acceptable
criteria.assessment_question: Does the framework define and require the implementation of safety mitigations along the entire model lifecycle that are appropriate to identified systemic risks, sufficiently robust under adversarial pressure, and taking into account the model’s release and distribution strategy, with the objective of ensuring that systemic risks are acceptable?
expected_evidence: The framework describes categories or types of safety mitigations intended to address systemic risks.
The framework explains that safety mitigations are designed to be robust under adversarial pressure, such as attempts to bypass or subvert them.
The framework indicates that safety mitigations take into account the model's release and distribution strategy.
The framework provides examples of safety mitigation approaches, such as e.g. input or output filtering, behaviour modification, staged access, or other emerging safety techniques.
The framework indicates that safety mitigations are considered and adapted across the model lifecycle.
criteria.reasoning: Indicators 2 (robustness under adversarial pressure), 4 (concrete mitigation examples), and 5 (lifecycle monitoring/adaptation) are supported by evidence. Indicators 1 (explicit taxonomy/categories of mitigations) and 3 (formal release/distribution linkage) are not clearly addressed, and their absence cannot be offset by thematic alignment.
key_aligned_concepts: Lifecycle-spanning safety risk management
Adversarial robustness and security/resilience
Mitigation practices including monitoring and human intervention
decisive_gaps_or_divergences: Explicit categories/types of safety mitigations (formal taxonomy) are not described.
A formal mechanism linking mitigations to the model’s release and distribution strategy is not defined.
Concrete mitigation approaches are not fully enumerated in the framework.

alignment_findings.assessment_question_answer: Yes — the text discusses lifecycle-spanning safety risk management, including early planning, ongoing monitoring and intervention, and robustness against adversarial conditions, aligning with the requirement to implement mitigations across the model lifecycle, though it does not explicitly enumerate mitigation categories or a formal release/distribution strategy.
alignment_findings.alignment_summary: The text supports lifecycle risk management and adversarial robustness as conceptual foundations, with examples such as monitoring and human intervention; however, it lacks explicit mitigation categorization and a dedicated release/distribution framework.

evidence_citations.quote: Robustness or generalizability is defined as the 'ability of a system to maintain its level of performance under a variety of circumstances' (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Robustness is a goal for appropriate system functionality in a broad set of conditions and circumstances, including uses of AI systems not initially anticipated. 3.3
Secure and Resilient
AI systems, as well as the ecosystems in which they are deployed, may be said to be resilient if they can withstand unexpected adverse events or unexpected changes in their environment or use – or if they can maintain their functions and structure in the face of internal
and external change and degrade safely and gracefully when this is necessary (Adapted
from: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Common security concerns relate to adversarial examples,
data poisoning, and the exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property
through AI system endpoints. AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and
availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may
be said to be secure. Guidelines in the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and Risk Management Framework are among those which are applicable here.
Security and resilience are related but distinct characteristics. While resilience is the ability to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event, security includes resilience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover
from attacks. Resilience relates to robustness and goes beyond the provenance of the data
to encompass unexpected or adversarial use (or abuse or misuse) of the model or data.

Robustness or generalizability is defined as the “ability of a system to maintain its level
of performance under a variety of circumstances” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Robustness is a goal for appropriate system functionality in a broad set of conditions and
circumstances, including uses of AI systems not initially anticipated. Robustness requires
not only that the system perform exactly as it does under expected uses, but also that it
should perform in ways that minimize potential harms to people if it is operating in an
unexpected setting.
Validity and reliability for deployed AI systems are often assessed by ongoing testing or
monitoring that confirms a system is performing as intended. Measurement of validity,
accuracy, robustness, and reliability contribute to trustworthiness and should take into consideration that certain types of failures can cause greater harm. AI risk management efforts
should prioritize the minimization of potential negative impacts, and may need to include
human intervention in cases where the AI system cannot detect or correct errors.
3.2
Safe
AI systems should “not under defined conditions, lead to a state in which human life,
health, property, or the environment is endangered” (Source: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Safe
operation of AI systems is improved through:
• responsible design, development, and deployment practices;
• clear information to deployers on responsible use of the system;

safety in fields such as transportation and healthcare, and align with existing sector- or
application-specific guidelines or standards.
3.3
Secure and Resilient
AI systems, as well as the ecosystems in which they are deployed, may be said to be resilient if they can withstand unexpected adverse events or unexpected changes in their environment or use – or if they can maintain their functions and structure in the face of internal
and external change and degrade safely and gracefully when this is necessary (Adapted
from: ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). Common security concerns relate to adversarial examples,
data poisoning, and the exfiltration of models, training data, or other intellectual property
through AI system endpoints. AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and
availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may
be said to be secure. Guidelines in the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and Risk Management Framework are among those which are applicable here.
Security and resilience are related but distinct characteristics. While resilience is the ability to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event, security includes resilience but also encompasses protocols to avoid, protect against, respond to, or recover
from attacks. Resilience relates to robustness and goes beyond the provenance of the data
to encompass unexpected or adversarial use (or abuse or misuse) of the model or data.

frameworks based on the domain addressed – and because AI risk management calls for

At the same time, guidance available before publication of this AI RMF does not comprehensively address many AI system risks. For example, existing frameworks and guidance

Part 2 comprises the “Core” of the Framework. It describes four specific functions to help
organizations address the risks of AI systems in practice. These functions – GOVERN,
MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE – are broken down further into categories and subcategories. While GOVERN applies to all stages of organizations’ AI risk management processes and procedures, the MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions can be applied in AI
system-specific contexts and at specific stages of the AI lifecycle.
Additional resources related to the Framework are included in the AI RMF Playbook,
which is available via the NIST AI RMF website:
https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework.
Development of the AI RMF by NIST in collaboration with the private and public sectors is directed and consistent with its broader AI efforts called for by the National AI
Initiative Act of 2020, the National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence recommendations, and the Plan for Federal Engagement in Developing Technical Standards and
Related Tools. Engagement with the AI community during this Framework’s development
– via responses to a formal Request for Information, three widely attended workshops,
public comments on a concept paper and two drafts of the Framework, discussions at multiple public forums, and many small group meetings – has informed development of the AI
RMF 1.0 as well as AI research and development and evaluation conducted by NIST and

the effectiveness of testing and can mitigate internal biases and potential conflicts of interest.
Where tradeoffs among the trustworthy characteristics arise, measurement provides a traceable basis to inform management decisions. Options may include recalibration, impact
mitigation, or removal of the system from design, development, production, or use, as well
as a range of compensating, detective, deterrent, directive, and recovery controls.
After completing the MEASURE function, objective, repeatable, or scalable test, evaluation,
verification, and validation (TEVV) processes including metrics, methods, and methodologies are in place, followed, and documented. Metrics and measurement methodologies
should adhere to scientific, legal, and ethical norms and be carried out in an open and transparent process. New types of measurement, qualitative and quantitative, may need to be
developed. The degree to which each measurement type provides unique and meaningful
information to the assessment of AI risks should be considered. Framework users will enhance their capacity to comprehensively evaluate system trustworthiness, identify and track
existing and emergent risks, and verify efficacy of the metrics. Measurement outcomes will
be utilized in the MANAGE function to assist risk monitoring and response efforts. It is incumbent on Framework users to continue applying the MEASURE function to AI systems
as knowledge, methodologies, risks, and impacts evolve over time.

criteria.title: Model description
criteria.requirement: Describe, in the Model Report, the model’s characteristics and intended behaviour, including a high-level description of the model, its intended and actual uses, version differences, and a model specification explaining how the model is intended to operate.
criteria.assessment_question: Does the Model Report describe the model’s architecture, capabilities, propensities, and affordances, its intended and actual uses, differences between model versions, and its intended behaviour (including principles, refusal topics, and system prompt or references thereto)?
expected_evidence: The Model Report provides a high-level description of the model’s architecture, capabilities, propensities, and affordances, and how it differs from other models made available by the provider.
The Model Report describes how the model has been used and how it is intended to be used, including relevant use contexts.
The Model Report identifies model versions that are or will be made available on the market and explains relevant differences, including differences in systemic risks or mitigations.

The Model Report includes or references a model specification describing how the model is intended to operate, including guiding principles, prioritisation of instructions, refusal topics, and the system prompt (or a valid reference to it).

1.2.3
Risk Prioritization
Attempting to eliminate negative risk entirely can be counterproductive in practice because
not all incidents and failures can be eliminated. Unrealistic expectations about risk may
lead organizations to allocate resources in a manner that makes risk triage inefficient or
impractical or wastes scarce resources. A risk management culture can help organizations
recognize that not all AI risks are the same, and resources can be allocated purposefully.
Actionable risk management efforts lay out clear guidelines for assessing trustworthiness
of each AI system an organization develops or deploys. Policies and resources should be
prioritized based on the assessed risk level and potential impact of an AI system. The extent
to which an AI system may be customized or tailored to the specific context of use by the
AI deployer can be a contributing factor.

criteria.title: Risk documentation
criteria.requirement: Describe in the Model Report how the systemic risk framework has been applied to the model, including reported results of systemic risk identification, analysis, modelling, estimation, evaluations, implemented safety and security mitigations, their limitations, and planned future developments.
criteria.assessment_question: What must the Model Report document regarding systemic risk identification, modelling, and estimates, including model evaluation results with random input/output samples, comparisons between safety-mitigated and fully elicited model versions, independent external evaluator access, Security Goal and mitigation limitations, and planned future model capabilities over the next six months?
expected_evidence: The Model Report describes the reported results of systemic risk identification and analysis, including assumptions, uncertainties, and links to the risk types defined in the framework.
The Model Report explains the reported outcomes of systemic risk modelling and estimation, including how risks are characterised and compared with and without mitigations.
The Model Report summarises relevant model evaluation approaches and results used to understand systemic risks, including illustrative examples or references.
The Model Report describes implemented safety mitigations and their limitations, and explains how they align with the framework’s safety requirements.
The Model Report describes the Security Goal and implemented security mitigations, including alignment with defined mitigation objectives or justified alternatives.
The Model Report includes a high-level forward-looking description of planned model developments and anticipated changes to capabilities, risks, and mitigations.
criteria.reasoning: Five of six expected indicators are clearly present (identification/analysis results with assumptions and risk links; modelling/estimation outcomes; evaluation approaches with TEVV; safety mitigations and their limits; security goal and mitigations). The sixth indicator—forward-looking six-month capability plan—is missing, and two alignment-influencing items from the gap analysis (random input/output samples reporting and independent external evaluator access) are not explicitly described. These gaps cannot be compensated by thematic overlap.
key_aligned_concepts: Systemic risk identification and analysis via MAP framework
Safety and security mitigations and their documentation
Forward-looking model developments and planned changes
TEVV metrics, evaluation approaches, and risk management
Versioning, traceability, and governance documentation

evidence_citations.quote: MAP 5: Impacts to individuals, groups, communities, organizations, and society are characterized. MAP 5.1: Likelihood and magnitude of each identified impact (both potentially beneficial and harmful) based on expected use, past uses of AI systems in similar contexts, public incident reports, feedback from those external to the team that developed or deployed the AI system, or other data are identified and documented. MAP 4: Risks and benefits are mapped for all components of the AI system including third-party software and data. MAP 4.1: Approaches for mapping AI technology and legal risks of its components – including the use of third-party data or software – are in place, followed, and documented, as are risks of infringement of a third party’s intellectual property or other rights. MAP 4.2: Internal risk controls for components of the AI system, including third-party AI technologies, are identified and documented.

criteria.requirement: Describe how the Model Report provides or references any available external reports from independent external model evaluators (Appendix 3.5) and independent external security reviews (Appendix 4.5), subject to confidentiality and evaluator control of publication, and how the report addresses cases where no external evaluator was involved or where evaluator selection must be justified.

If at least one independent external evaluator was involved, the Model Report explains the choice of evaluator with reference to qualification criteria (e.g., domain expertise, technical evaluation experience, appropriate security protocols, confidentiality protections).

and inaccurate but secure, privacy-enhanced, and transparent systems are all undesirable. A comprehensive approach to risk management calls for balancing tradeoffs

or deploy an AI system should be based on a contextual assessment of trustworthiness characteristics and the relative risks, impacts, costs, and benefits, and informed

The Model Report describes information relevant to assessing changes in mitigation effectiveness (e.g., reduced human legibility of chain-of-thought or other safety-relevant properties).
The Model Report describes training techniques that materially improve the efficiency or feasibility of training (e.g., distributed or large-scale training), where applicable.

addition, measurement approaches can be oversimplified, gamed, lack critical nuance, become relied upon in unexpected ways, or fail to account for differences in affected groups

Approaches for measuring impacts on a population work best if they recognize that contexts
